payload.title: Poetry Analysis: The Darkling Thrush
payload.set_intro:
Public-domain source text — Thomas Hardy, The Darkling Thrush, Poems of the Past and the Present (Gutenberg eBook #3168). The file does not state the printing, so the exact edition is UNVERIFIED. Poem dated 'December 1900' and first published in 1900-1901; the collection is dated 1902
The Darkling Thrush
by Thomas Hardy
The following poem is by Thomas Hardy (1902).

```passage
I LEANT upon a coppice gate
When Frost was spectre-gray,
And Winter’s dregs made desolate
The weakening eye of day.
The tangled bine-stems scored the sky
Like strings from broken lyres,
And all mankind that haunted nigh
Had sought their household fires.

The land’s sharp features seemed to be
The Century’s corpse outleant,
His crypt the cloudy canopy,
The wind his death-lament.
The ancient pulse of germ and birth
Was shrunken hard and dry,
And every spirit upon earth
Seemed fervourless as I.

At once a voice outburst among
The bleak twigs overhead
In a full-hearted evensong
Of joy illimited;
An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small,
In blast-beruffled plume,
Had chosen thus to fling his soul
Upon the growing gloom.

So little cause for carollings
Of such ecstatic sound
Was written on terrestrial things
Afar or nigh around,
That I could think there trembled through
His happy good-night air
Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew
And I was unaware.
```

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
The following poem is "The Darkling Thrush" by Thomas Hardy (1900). In this poem, the speaker describes standing alone at a gate on a desolate winter evening, seeing the landscape as the corpse of a dying century, until the sudden song of an old, frail thrush interrupts his gloom.

Read the poem closely. Then write an essay in which you analyze how Thomas Hardy uses poetic elements and techniques to convey the speaker's tense, divided response to a joy he hears but cannot share, as a world he has pictured as dead is challenged by a hope he can only guess at and never fully take on as his own.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that offers a defensible interpretation of the poem.
- Use specific evidence from the poem, and explain how that evidence supports your line of reasoning.
- Explain how multiple poetic elements and techniques contribute to the meaning you describe.
- Write clearly, with appropriate grammar and punctuation.
parts.model_answer:
Hardy's speaker begins the poem sure that he is reading the world correctly. The landscape is dead, the century is dead, and everyone else feels as hollow as he does. The thrush does not prove him wrong so much as it shows him where his vision stops. Through death imagery that turns out to be partly projection, a sharp turn that sets the bird's frail body against its unlimited song, and a final stanza full of hedges, Hardy shows a speaker who is shaken out of his certainty but can only admit hope as something another creature has. He can see the joy, but he never gets to feel it.

The first two stanzas build a world of decay so complete that it starts to look suspicious. The frost is "spectre-gray," the sun is "The weakening eye of day," and the vines look "Like strings from broken lyres." That simile matters, because a lyre is the classic instrument of poetry, so even music has already been broken before the thrush appears. In stanza two the metaphor grows into a full funeral, with the land as the century's "corpse outleant," the sky as "His crypt the cloudy canopy," and the wind as a "death-lament." The extended conceit is so careful that it becomes clear the speaker is arranging the scene and not just recording it. The stanza ends with "Seemed fervourless as I," and the word "Seemed" gives him away. He measures "every spirit upon earth" against his own mood, so the deadness of the world is at least partly his own deadness spread across it.

That is why the turn in stanza three matters so much. "At once a voice outburst" breaks the slow, heavy pace of the earlier lines, and the bird's song is described in language that refuses limits: "full-hearted evensong," "Of joy illimited." Hardy then sets this against the body producing the song: "An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small." The ironic contrast makes the bird belong to the dying world the speaker described, old and battered "In blast-beruffled plume," and yet it sings. The verb in "fling his soul" makes the singing a choice and not an instinct, almost reckless, thrown "Upon the growing gloom." The bird faces the same evidence the speaker does and makes a different decision about it, and that difference is what challenges him.

The last stanza is where the speaker's divided response is clearest, mostly through grammar. He admits there is "So little cause for carollings" written on "terrestrial things," so he never takes back his reading of the landscape. Instead he moves the hope somewhere he cannot check. "I could think there trembled through" is a stack of qualifiers: a conditional verb, a verb of guessing, and "trembled," which makes the hope faint and unsteady. Then "Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew" leaves it vague and hands the knowledge to the bird. The religious vocabulary throughout, "evensong," "carollings," "blessed Hope," brings in the language of Christian faith, but the speaker uses it from the outside, the way someone might describe a church service they are watching through a window. The capital H makes Hope sound like a doctrine, yet the poem ends on "And I was unaware." Rhyming "knew" with "through" and setting "air" against "unaware" makes the gap audible: the knowledge belongs to the bird, and the speaker is left with the absence of it.

So the poem is neither simply hopeful nor simply bleak. The thrush cracks the speaker's confident picture of a dead world by showing that his "fervourless" view was a way of seeing and not the whole truth. But honesty keeps him from claiming a hope he does not have. Hardy's ending is moving because the speaker is willing to admit joy exists while saying plainly that it is not his.

rubric_rows.criterion: A defensible thesis makes an arguable claim about how the speaker responds to the gap between the dead landscape and the thrush's joy. Examples: the speaker admits a hope exists but places it outside himself, or the song unsettles his despair without overturning it. Theses that only summarize (a sad man hears a bird and feels better), only list devices, or say the poem is simply hopeful or simply despairing, with no tension, do not earn the point. The thesis may be more than one sentence but must appear in one place.

Strong responses trace the movement across the poem. The first two stanzas build a world of decay through death imagery (spectre-gray frost, corpse, crypt, death-lament, broken lyres). Stanza three turns with 'At once' and sets the bird's frailty ('aged,' 'frail, gaunt, and small') against the unlimited joy of its song. The last stanza hedges with 'So little cause,' 'I could think,' 'Some,' and 'unaware.' Commentary should explain how each choice builds the divided attitude, for example how 'fervourless as I' shows the speaker reading his own mood into the world, or how 'fling his soul' makes the song a deliberate act of will. A 4 needs well-chosen evidence and commentary that keeps tying details back to the line of reasoning. A 3 explains some evidence but is uneven. A 2 mostly summarizes or names devices with little explanation. A 1 offers little relevant evidence.

Sophistication might look like this: seeing that the bleak landscape is partly the speaker's projection, so the bird's song tests his way of seeing as well as the world itself. Exploring the religious language (evensong, carollings, blessed Hope) and its uneasy fit with a speaker who stays 'unaware.' Reading the ending's grammar as making hope an inference the speaker never reaches himself. Or noticing the irony that the most frail creature in the poem is the one who sings with full heart. The insight must run through the whole argument, not appear in one sentence or rest on unsupported claims about the poet's life or beliefs.

Sample essay (mid; scored 4/6: thesis 1, evidence 3, sophistication 0)
In "The Darkling Thrush," Thomas Hardy shows a speaker who is pulled in two directions. He hears a joyful song that goes against everything he sees, but he cannot make himself feel that joy. Hardy uses imagery, diction, and the structure of the stanzas to show that the speaker admits hope might exist while keeping it outside of himself.

The first two stanzas build a world that is dying. Hardy describes the frost as "spectre-gray," which makes the winter feel like a ghost and not just weather. The "tangled bine-stems" are compared to "strings from broken lyres," and this suggests that music and beauty have been broken. People have also gone inside to their "household fires," so the speaker is completely alone. In the second stanza the land is the "Century's corpse," with the clouds as his "crypt" and the wind as his "death-lament." All of this death imagery makes the reader feel how hopeless the speaker is. The line "fervourless as I" is important because it shows he thinks every spirit on earth feels as empty as he does, so he may be projecting his own mood onto the world.

The poem turns at the start of the third stanza with "At once." The sudden phrase interrupts the quiet gloom and the song bursts out in "a full-hearted evensong / Of joy illimited." The word "evensong" gives the song a religious feeling. However, the thrush itself is described as "aged," "frail, gaunt, and small," which is the opposite of the big joy it sings. This contrast is ironic, because the weakest thing in the poem is the one that is joyful. The bird chooses to "fling his soul" into the gloom, which makes it sound like a deliberate act and not just something natural.

In the last stanza the speaker's response is divided. He says there is "so little cause" for the song, so he does not see a reason for joy in the world around him. Then he says "I could think" that there is "some blessed Hope" the bird knows about. The words "could" and "some" are uncertain, and he ends with "unaware," which means he is still outside the hope. The rhyme scheme stays the same and the stanzas are regular, so the poem sounds controlled, but the speaker's feelings are not settled.

In conclusion, Hardy uses death imagery, the contrast of the small bird with its big song, and hesitant word choices to show a speaker who hears hope but cannot feel it. The song challenges his despair a little, but it does not fully change him, and that is what makes the poem tense.
- Row A: "the speaker admits hope might exist while keeping it outside of himself" - This is a defensible, arguable claim that answers the prompt by naming the gap between the speaker and the hope. It earns the thesis point, though the thesis is stated plainly and the first sentence is somewhat generic.
- Row B: "The first two stanzas build a world that is dying." - This starts a clear line of reasoning that follows the poem's movement. It is specific enough to organize the evidence, but the paragraph relies on listing images.
- Row B: "All of this death imagery makes the reader feel how hopeless the speaker is." - The commentary is general and repetitive. It names the imagery and gives its effect without explaining how particular words such as 'crypt' or 'death-lament' work. This keeps the row from reaching the top score.
- Row C: "so he may be projecting his own mood onto the world" - This is a good insight about projection, and it is tied to a specific quotation. It appears in one sentence and is not developed or carried through the rest of the essay, so it does not earn sophistication.
- Row B: "This contrast is ironic, because the weakest thing in the poem is the one that is joyful." - This explains how the frail diction sets up irony and connects to the argument. It is relevant commentary and one of the stronger moments. The 'fling his soul' point is a brief but useful observation about will.
- Row B: "The words "could" and "some" are uncertain, and he ends with "unaware,"" - Specific evidence for the hedging in the last stanza, directly supporting the thesis about hope staying outside the speaker. The commentary is brief and does not examine the grammar or the religious language in 'blessed Hope' for deeper complexity.
- Row C: "The rhyme scheme stays the same and the stanzas are regular, so the poem sounds controlled, but the speaker's feelings are not settled." - This attempts a formal technique, but it is thin and asserted without evidence of the actual rhyme pattern. It is a missed chance to build a more complex argument about form and feeling.

Sample essay (low; scored 2/6: thesis 0, evidence 2, sophistication 0)
In the poem The Darkling Thrush by Thomas Hardy, the speaker is standing at a gate on a cold winter evening and he feels sad about the world. Then a thrush starts singing and the speaker is surprised. Hardy uses imagery, diction and structure to show this and the poem is about sadness and hope.

In the first stanza the speaker describes the winter scene in a very gloomy way. He says the frost was "spectre-gray" which makes it sound like a ghost. The "tangled bine-stems" are like "strings from broken lyres" so the world is broken and has no music. Everyone has gone inside to their fires so he is alone. This shows that the speaker is depressed and the setting is dark.

In the second stanza the land is compared to "The Century's corpse" and the wind is the "death-lament." This is personification and it shows that the century is dying. The speaker says every spirit is "fervourless as I" which means he feels like everything is dead like he is. The poem is set in 1900 so it is the end of a century which is why Hardy uses this.

Then in the third stanza a thrush sings. The words "At once" show it is sudden. The bird is "aged" and "frail, gaunt, and small" but sings a happy song anyway. This is a contrast because the bird looks weak but is joyful. The song is called an "evensong" which is like a church song.

In the last stanza the speaker thinks the bird might know some "blessed Hope" that he doesn't know about. So at the end he is not sure. Overall Hardy shows through his word choice that the speaker is sad but the bird gives him a little bit of hope, even though he does not fully have it.
- Row A: "the poem is about sadness and hope" - The thesis only names a general subject (sadness and hope) and lists devices; it makes no arguable claim about the speaker's divided response or the gap between his gloom and the bird's joy, so it earns no thesis credit.
- Row B: "This shows that the speaker is depressed and the setting is dark." - Quotes specific phrases like 'spectre-gray' and 'broken lyres' but the commentary stays general; it says the scene is gloomy without explaining how the imagery builds the speaker's mood or sets up the later tension.
- Row B: "This is personification and it shows that the century is dying." - Names a technique and gives a simple meaning, a start at commentary, but does not connect it to the speaker's divided response or trace how death imagery sets up the thrush's contrast.
- Row C: "which is like a church song" - Notes the religious word 'evensong' but does not explore its uneasy fit with a speaker who stays unaware; the observation is left undeveloped, so no sophistication credit.
- Row C: "So at the end he is not sure." - Touches the hedged ending ('some blessed Hope') but only in summary; it does not analyze the tentative grammar or the speaker's inability to share the hope, and the conclusion remains a general statement.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No defensible thesis: the response only restates the prompt, summarizes or describes the text, makes a comment that does not answer the prompt, or never states an interpretation that needs to be defended.
descriptors.1: The response states a defensible interpretation that answers the prompt (it may take more than one sentence and may appear anywhere in the essay).

The thesis may be more than one sentence but must appear in one place.

rows.name: Evidence and commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the prompt, repeats given information, or offers irrelevant material; no usable evidence or commentary.
descriptors.1: Evidence is mostly general; the response summarizes or paraphrases and does not explain how the evidence supports an argument.
descriptors.2: Some specific, relevant evidence, mixed with generalities. Explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning is established or it is faulty.
descriptors.3: Specific evidence for the claims in a line of reasoning, and explains how some of that evidence supports the line of reasoning, including how at least one literary element or technique contributes to meaning.
descriptors.4: Specific evidence supports every claim in a line of reasoning, the commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports it, and it explains how multiple literary elements or techniques contribute to meaning. Errors that interfere with communication prevent this level.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Does not meet the criteria for the point: contextualizing is limited to sweeping generalities, other readings are only hinted at, complexity is oversimplified, or elaborate language does not advance the argument.
descriptors.1: Shows sophistication of thought or develops a complex literary argument, sustained through the essay (not a phrase): explores tensions or complexities in the text, situates the interpretation in a broader context, accounts for alternative interpretations, or uses a consistently vivid and persuasive style.

defensible_positions: The speaker admits hope may exist but cannot share it, so the poem ends in a kind of isolation, not consolation.
The bleak first half shows the speaker projecting his own lifelessness onto the world ('fervourless as I'), and the thrush exposes the limits of that view.
The thrush's frailty makes its joy an act of will rather than a response to its conditions, so hope in the poem is something chosen, not something earned or proven.
The religious language near the end opens the idea of faith, but the hedging grammar keeps the speaker at a skeptical distance from it.
The poem moves from certainty about decay to uncertainty about hope, so the speaker's real change is from closed despair to open doubt.

devices.effect: The capitalized, ghostly Frost makes the setting seem haunted and lifeless from the start, which sets up the death imagery.
Comparing the vines to broken lyres suggests music and poetry have failed. This sets up the irony of the song that follows.
Turning the whole landscape into a burial scene (corpse, crypt, death-lament) makes the despair total and seemingly final.
'Seemed' and the comparison to 'I' show that the speaker reads the world through his own mood, so the bleakness is partly his projection.

devices.quote: At once a voice outburst among
devices.effect: The sudden 'At once' and the energetic 'outburst' break into the slow, deathly mood and start the poem's central conflict.

devices.quote: An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small,
devices.effect: The bird's frailty is set against its 'joy illimited.' Its joy cannot come from its condition, which makes the song seem willed or mysterious.
The repeated g sounds weigh the darkness down against the bird's defiant act of flinging its song into it.

devices.quote: That I could think there trembled through
devices.effect: The conditional, hedged phrasing presents hope only as a possibility the speaker guesses at, not a conviction he holds.
The final line names a hope and in the same breath shuts the speaker out of it, so the ending stays divided.

common_pitfalls: Reading the poem as a simple shift from sadness to happiness and ignoring the speaker's final 'unaware.'
Summarizing the stanzas in order without connecting the details to the speaker's divided attitude.
Listing devices (alliteration, personification) without explaining what they do.
Building the argument on outside claims about the poet's beliefs or the historical era that the text does not support.
Treating the thrush purely as a symbol and ignoring the stress on its physical frailty.

The first two stanzas build a world of decay so complete that it starts to look suspicious. The frost is "spectre-gray," the sun is "The weakening eye of day," and the vines look "Like strings from broken lyres." That simile matters, because a lyre is the classic instrument of poetry, so even music has already been broken before the thrush appears. In stanza two the metaphor grows into a full funeral, with the land as the century's "corpse outleant," the sky as "His crypt the cloudy canopy," and the wind as a "death-lament." The extended conceit is so careful that it becomes clear the speaker is arranging the scene and not just recording it. The stanza ends with "Seemed fervourless as I," and the word "Seemed" gives him away. He measures "every spirit upon earth" against his own mood, so the deadness of the world is at least partly his own deadness spread across it.

That is why the turn in stanza three matters so much. "At once a voice outburst" breaks the slow, heavy pace of the earlier lines, and the bird's song is described in language that refuses limits: "full-hearted evensong," "Of joy illimited." Hardy then sets this against the body producing the song: "An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small." The ironic contrast makes the bird belong to the dying world the speaker described, old and battered "In blast-beruffled plume," and yet it sings. The verb in "fling his soul" makes the singing a choice and not an instinct, almost reckless, thrown "Upon the growing gloom." The bird faces the same evidence the speaker does and makes a different decision about it, and that difference is what challenges him.

The last stanza is where the speaker's divided response is clearest, mostly through grammar. He admits there is "So little cause for carollings" written on "terrestrial things," so he never takes back his reading of the landscape. Instead he moves the hope somewhere he cannot check. "I could think there trembled through" is a stack of qualifiers: a conditional verb, a verb of guessing, and "trembled," which makes the hope faint and unsteady. Then "Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew" leaves it vague and hands the knowledge to the bird. The religious vocabulary throughout, "evensong," "carollings," "blessed Hope," brings in the language of Christian faith, but the speaker uses it from the outside, the way someone might describe a church service they are watching through a window. The capital H makes Hope sound like a doctrine, yet the poem ends on "And I was unaware." Rhyming "knew" with "through" and setting "air" against "unaware" makes the gap audible: the knowledge belongs to the bird, and the speaker is left with the absence of it.

So the poem is neither simply hopeful nor simply bleak. The thrush cracks the speaker's confident picture of a dead world by showing that his "fervourless" view was a way of seeing and not the whole truth. But honesty keeps him from claiming a hope he does not have. Hardy's ending is moving because the speaker is willing to admit joy exists while saying plainly that it is not his.

annotations.quote: He can see the joy, but he never gets to feel it.
annotations.comment: This finishes a thesis that makes a defensible claim with real tension in it. The song shakes the speaker but only gets him to see hope in someone else. The thesis also sets up the order of the essay: projection, then the turn, then the hedging at the end.

annotations.quote: a lyre is the classic instrument of poetry, so even music has already been broken
annotations.comment: This goes past naming the simile and explains its effect. It links the image to the song that comes later, which keeps the argument going.
Close reading of one word supports the claim that the dead world is partly the speaker's projection, as the task-specific rubric suggests.

annotations.quote: The verb in "fling his soul" makes the singing a choice and not an instinct
annotations.comment: This explains how a word choice builds meaning. It treats the bird's song as an act of will, and that ties back to the challenge the speaker faces.

annotations.quote: "I could think there trembled through" is a stack of qualifiers
annotations.comment: This breaks down the grammar and diction of the hedging and explains how each part keeps hope uncertain. Together with the rhyme analysis, it shows several techniques working together, which is what a 4 needs.

annotations.quote: the way someone might describe a church service they are watching through a window
annotations.comment: This explores how the religious language sits uneasily with a speaker who stays 'unaware.' It is one of several sophisticated threads, along with projection and irony, that run through the whole essay.

annotations.quote: showing that his "fervourless" view was a way of seeing and not the whole truth
annotations.comment: The essay carries its projection reading through to the end, so the song tests the speaker's way of seeing as well as the world itself. Because this insight runs through the whole argument, it earns the sophistication point.

samples.essay:
In "The Darkling Thrush," Thomas Hardy shows a speaker who is pulled in two directions. He hears a joyful song that goes against everything he sees, but he cannot make himself feel that joy. Hardy uses imagery, diction, and the structure of the stanzas to show that the speaker admits hope might exist while keeping it outside of himself.

The first two stanzas build a world that is dying. Hardy describes the frost as "spectre-gray," which makes the winter feel like a ghost and not just weather. The "tangled bine-stems" are compared to "strings from broken lyres," and this suggests that music and beauty have been broken. People have also gone inside to their "household fires," so the speaker is completely alone. In the second stanza the land is the "Century's corpse," with the clouds as his "crypt" and the wind as his "death-lament." All of this death imagery makes the reader feel how hopeless the speaker is. The line "fervourless as I" is important because it shows he thinks every spirit on earth feels as empty as he does, so he may be projecting his own mood onto the world.

The poem turns at the start of the third stanza with "At once." The sudden phrase interrupts the quiet gloom and the song bursts out in "a full-hearted evensong / Of joy illimited." The word "evensong" gives the song a religious feeling. However, the thrush itself is described as "aged," "frail, gaunt, and small," which is the opposite of the big joy it sings. This contrast is ironic, because the weakest thing in the poem is the one that is joyful. The bird chooses to "fling his soul" into the gloom, which makes it sound like a deliberate act and not just something natural.

In the last stanza the speaker's response is divided. He says there is "so little cause" for the song, so he does not see a reason for joy in the world around him. Then he says "I could think" that there is "some blessed Hope" the bird knows about. The words "could" and "some" are uncertain, and he ends with "unaware," which means he is still outside the hope. The rhyme scheme stays the same and the stanzas are regular, so the poem sounds controlled, but the speaker's feelings are not settled.

In conclusion, Hardy uses death imagery, the contrast of the small bird with its big song, and hesitant word choices to show a speaker who hears hope but cannot feel it. The song challenges his despair a little, but it does not fully change him, and that is what makes the poem tense.

annotations.quote: the speaker admits hope might exist while keeping it outside of himself
annotations.comment: This is a defensible, arguable claim that answers the prompt by naming the gap between the speaker and the hope. It earns the thesis point, though the thesis is stated plainly and the first sentence is somewhat generic.

annotations.quote: The first two stanzas build a world that is dying.
annotations.comment: This starts a clear line of reasoning that follows the poem's movement. It is specific enough to organize the evidence, but the paragraph relies on listing images.

annotations.quote: All of this death imagery makes the reader feel how hopeless the speaker is.
annotations.comment: The commentary is general and repetitive. It names the imagery and gives its effect without explaining how particular words such as 'crypt' or 'death-lament' work. This keeps the row from reaching the top score.

annotations.quote: so he may be projecting his own mood onto the world
annotations.comment: This is a good insight about projection, and it is tied to a specific quotation. It appears in one sentence and is not developed or carried through the rest of the essay, so it does not earn sophistication.

annotations.quote: This contrast is ironic, because the weakest thing in the poem is the one that is joyful.
annotations.comment: This explains how the frail diction sets up irony and connects to the argument. It is relevant commentary and one of the stronger moments. The 'fling his soul' point is a brief but useful observation about will.

annotations.quote: The words "could" and "some" are uncertain, and he ends with "unaware,"
annotations.comment: Specific evidence for the hedging in the last stanza, directly supporting the thesis about hope staying outside the speaker. The commentary is brief and does not examine the grammar or the religious language in 'blessed Hope' for deeper complexity.

annotations.quote: The rhyme scheme stays the same and the stanzas are regular, so the poem sounds controlled, but the speaker's feelings are not settled.
annotations.comment: This attempts a formal technique, but it is thin and asserted without evidence of the actual rhyme pattern. It is a missed chance to build a more complex argument about form and feeling.

samples.essay:
In the poem The Darkling Thrush by Thomas Hardy, the speaker is standing at a gate on a cold winter evening and he feels sad about the world. Then a thrush starts singing and the speaker is surprised. Hardy uses imagery, diction and structure to show this and the poem is about sadness and hope.

In the first stanza the speaker describes the winter scene in a very gloomy way. He says the frost was "spectre-gray" which makes it sound like a ghost. The "tangled bine-stems" are like "strings from broken lyres" so the world is broken and has no music. Everyone has gone inside to their fires so he is alone. This shows that the speaker is depressed and the setting is dark.

In the second stanza the land is compared to "The Century's corpse" and the wind is the "death-lament." This is personification and it shows that the century is dying. The speaker says every spirit is "fervourless as I" which means he feels like everything is dead like he is. The poem is set in 1900 so it is the end of a century which is why Hardy uses this.

Then in the third stanza a thrush sings. The words "At once" show it is sudden. The bird is "aged" and "frail, gaunt, and small" but sings a happy song anyway. This is a contrast because the bird looks weak but is joyful. The song is called an "evensong" which is like a church song.

In the last stanza the speaker thinks the bird might know some "blessed Hope" that he doesn't know about. So at the end he is not sure. Overall Hardy shows through his word choice that the speaker is sad but the bird gives him a little bit of hope, even though he does not fully have it.

annotations.quote: the poem is about sadness and hope
annotations.comment: The thesis only names a general subject (sadness and hope) and lists devices; it makes no arguable claim about the speaker's divided response or the gap between his gloom and the bird's joy, so it earns no thesis credit.

annotations.quote: This shows that the speaker is depressed and the setting is dark.
annotations.comment: Quotes specific phrases like 'spectre-gray' and 'broken lyres' but the commentary stays general; it says the scene is gloomy without explaining how the imagery builds the speaker's mood or sets up the later tension.

annotations.quote: This is personification and it shows that the century is dying.
annotations.comment: Names a technique and gives a simple meaning, a start at commentary, but does not connect it to the speaker's divided response or trace how death imagery sets up the thrush's contrast.

annotations.quote: which is like a church song
annotations.comment: Notes the religious word 'evensong' but does not explore its uneasy fit with a speaker who stays unaware; the observation is left undeveloped, so no sophistication credit.

annotations.quote: So at the end he is not sure.
annotations.comment: Touches the hedged ending ('some blessed Hope') but only in summary; it does not analyze the tentative grammar or the speaker's inability to share the hope, and the conclusion remains a general statement.

blueprint.central_idea: Faced with a world he has imagined as dead, the speaker hears a frail bird sing with unlimited joy. He grants that a hope might exist, but only as something the bird seems to know and he does not.
blueprint.complexity: The shift in the poem is real but incomplete. The bleakness of the first half is partly the speaker's projection, the bird's joy has no visible cause, and the closing language reaches toward faith while the hedged grammar holds the speaker at a distance. Readers can argue for qualified hope, deepened isolation, or open doubt.
